extracted.intended_audience: researchers, journal editors, science journalists, and readers interested in research integrity and retractions
extracted.subtask_description: A weekend-read news roundup summarizing recent items related to research integrity, retractions, misconduct, and science journalism. Curates links and short excerpts highlighting problems (plagiarism, predatory journals, data errors, conflicts of interest, legal threats) and debates about standards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Plagiarism is unethical and undermines trust
rubrics_metrics.description: Examples such as 'The Co-Founder Of Snopes Wrote Dozens Of Plagiarized Articles For The Fact-Checking Site.' indicate that plagiarism by staff (including leaders/co‑founders) is a serious ethical failing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plagiarism in journalism or scholarship erodes public trust in fact‑checking and research institutions; organizations should have and enforce journalistic and academic ethics, and leadership is held to high standards. The page highlights reactions and community dismay as consequences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wilfully submitting to and publishing in predatory journals may constitute research misconduct
rubrics_metrics.description: The question is posed explicitly: 'Wilfully submitting to and publishing in predatory journals – a covert form of research misconduct?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The item frames intentional engagement with predatory publishers as potentially covert misconduct, sparking debate about culpability, institutional consequences, and how to classify such behavior (submission vs. acceptance vs. editorial participation).

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorial board membership with predatory publishers can be ethically problematic
rubrics_metrics.description: Commenters ask whether serving on editorial boards of publishers listed as predatory should be considered scientific misconduct.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Accepting editorial roles at predatory journals may signal willful association and merits scrutiny; institutions and faculty should consider advising against such memberships and clarify policies.

rubrics_metrics.name: Peer review should serve a substantive scholarly purpose rather than merely being administrative
rubrics_metrics.description: Quoted critique: 'In reality, peer-review is a purely administrative process that allows people to rise up the academic ladder. Whatever scholarly purpose it serves is secondary.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This highlights a standard that peer review ought to be meaningful quality control; if treated only as administrative, it fails its evaluative role. Journals and communities must ensure peer review performs substantive methodological and ethical checks.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authors must adequately study their work before publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted when authors 'admit they “published the paper without completely studying their work.”'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Publishing without fully studying or verifying results is a breach of research norms; authors are expected to perform necessary analyses and checks before submission, and failure may justify retraction or correction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Timely journal action and protection of critics is important
rubrics_metrics.description: Noted item: 'Critics face legal threats as journal takes more than three years to act.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals should respond promptly to credible concerns; lengthy inaction can expose critics to legal threats and undermine accountability. Editorial timeliness is part of responsible publishing practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Serious consequences (including legal/criminal) attach to falsifying clinical trial data
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported: a federal judge sentenced people to prison 'in connection with their participation in a conspiracy to falsify data related to clinical drug trials.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Fabrication or falsification of clinical trial data may trigger criminal prosecution and severe penalties; researchers and institutions must ensure data integrity and regulatory compliance in trials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Withholding care in clinical research is unethical
rubrics_metrics.description: Headline: 'Critics say a childhood asthma study unethically withheld care—and see a troubling trend.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Clinical studies must not deprive participants of necessary care; ethical oversight (IRBs, consent, safety protocols) is required, and failure to provide care constitutes serious misconduct.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data management errors (e.g., mangled gene names) compromise reproducibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported finding: '30% of published papers contain mangled gene names in supplementary data.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Poor data handling (spreadsheet conversions, naming errors) can corrupt results and supplementary materials; authors should use robust data management practices and check machine‑readable files to ensure reproducibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statistical concepts like 'statistical significance' have contested origins and implications
rubrics_metrics.description: 'How the strange idea of “statistical significance” was born.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Authors, reviewers, and readers should be aware of the historical and conceptual limits of p‑values/statistical significance and avoid overreliance on arbitrary thresholds when judging evidence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conflicts of interest and methodological issues can sully study credibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Item: 'Conflicts of interest and methodological issues sully a study…in the Journal of Autism and Developmental Disorders, autism researchers say.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Transparency about funding and conflicts and rigorous methodology are required to maintain credibility; undisclosed COIs or flawed methods undermine trust and may necessitate correction or retraction.

rubrics_metrics.name: Replications do not always straightforwardly increase trustworthiness
rubrics_metrics.description: Question posed: 'Does a successful replication always increase trustworthiness?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Replication outcomes must be interpreted in context (methods, populations, effect sizes); successful replication is important but not automatically definitive—nuance is needed when using replication to assess reliability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monitoring and detection tools (e.g., Twitter data) can spot publication problems early
rubrics_metrics.description: 'Can Twitter data help in spotting problems early with publications?'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Alternative data sources and social‑media monitoring may provide early signals of problems (errors, misconduct); such tools can complement formal peer review and post‑publication review processes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Persisting citations of retracted influential papers are a problem
rubrics_metrics.description: Item: 'Another look at citations of Wakefield’s retracted 1998 paper.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Retracted papers may continue to be cited and influence discourse; publishers, databases, and scholars should clearly flag retractions and correct the literature to limit ongoing harm.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predatory journals violate standard editorial and publishing practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Referenced: 'Violations of Standard Practices by Predatory Economics Journals.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Journals that do not adhere to accepted peer review, editorial oversight, and transparency should be recognized and avoided; institutions should educate researchers about identifying predatory outlets.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authorship and leadership must understand and follow domain‑specific ethics
rubrics_metrics.description: Comment: the plagiarizer 'was not a journalist, and didn’t really understand journalistic ethics.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contributors to a field (journalists, scientists) must learn and apply the relevant ethical standards; leaders have special responsibility to model and enforce ethics among staff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Journals and the literature should correct the record via retractions/withdrawals when warranted
rubrics_metrics.description: Multiple items: retractions, withdrawn COVID‑19 papers, authors retracting papers (e.g., 2014 Nature paper), Ivermectin meta‑analysis to be retracted/revised.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When errors, misconduct, or unreliable findings are identified, the appropriate corrective mechanisms (erratum, correction, retraction, expression of concern) should be used transparently and promptly to maintain literature integrity.
